title: Effect of Color Temperature and Illuminance on Psychology, Physiology, and Productivity: An Experimental Study
research_question: To research the effects of CCT and illuminance on human psychology, physiology, and work productivity and to propose a personalized lighting control schedule for offices.

participants.description: 34 males and 33 females in their 20s, NCKU students, corrected visual acuity between 1.0 and 1.2, no major organ diseases or physiological abnormalities, asked to get enough sleep and not take therapeutic drugs.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Smart lighting laboratory without daylight. Six fixed lighting conditions and two adjustable lighting modes. Fixed CCTs: 3000 K, 4000 K, 5500 K. Fixed Illuminances: 280 lux, 210 lux, 175 lux (Phase 1); 590 lux, 420 lux, 350 lux (Phase 2). EML values: 120 EML, 145 EML (Phase 1); 250 EML, 300 EML (Phase 2). Adjustable lighting initial states: 3000 K, 100 lux; 5500 K, 750 lux.

mechanisms: Higher illumination could reduce the sensations of discomfort.
Warm CCT (3000 K) makes subjects feel warmer, influencing comfort perception.
Sufficient EML (≥150) promotes alertness and activates anti-melanin hormone mechanisms, improving work efficiency.
implementation_implications: For user-controlled lighting, preset values of 4200 K CCT and 500 lux horizontal illumination are suggested, with a memory controller to record user adjustments.
For uncontrollable lighting, suggested settings are 3000 K CCT and 500 lux horizontal illumination.
For high-efficiency lighting, illumination must be >500 lux with ≥150 EML.
For healthy lighting, maintain ≥150 EML between 09:00-13:00, and reduce CCT after 20:00 to minimize blue light absorption.
For energy-saving, use intermittent lighting (5-10 min each hour) or combine with outdoor real-time monitoring to adjust artificial light by daylight.
Proposed comprehensive lighting control strategies for office spaces (8:00-17:00) based on productivity, circadian rhythm, and energy-saving, including fixed and adjustable modes.

limitations: The experiment used 60 min as a unit, which may not fully capture the long-term or chronic effects of lighting on human physiology, psychology, and work efficiency.
The experimental time could be expanded to an eight-hour workday or include night lighting behavior patterns for results closer to real situations.
Future work should be carried out in a field office to verify reproducibility and provide more detailed suggestions for actual offices.

paper_metadata.title: Effect of Color Temperature and Illuminance on Psychology, Physiology, and Productivity: An Experimental Study
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effect of Color Temperature and Illuminance on Psychology, Physiology, and Productivity: An Experimental Study
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In this study, we investigated the impact of the lighting environment on psychological perception, physiology, and productivity and then designed lighting control strategies based on the experimental results. The research was conducted in a smart lighting laboratory, and 67 subjects were tested in different illuminances and correlated color temperatures (CCTs). During the experiment, the physiological data of subjects were continuously recorded, while the psychology and productivity results were evaluated by questionnaires and working tests, respectively. The experimental results found that both illuminance and CCT could significantly influence the feeling of comfort and relaxation of the subjects. Warm CCT and higher illuminance (3000 K–590 lux) made subjects feel more comfortable. Productivity reached its maximum value with illuminance above 500 lux and equivalent melanopic lux (EML) higher than 150. The brain-wave and heart-rate changes did not have a close relationship with either illuminance or CCT, but the heart rate slightly increased in the adjustable lighting mode. Regardless of the initial value setting, the subjects preferred intermediate CCT (4200 K) and bright illumination (500 lux) after self-adjustment. Finally, we proposed three comprehensive lighting control strategies based on psychology, productivity, circadian rhythm, and energy-saving.
